Big idea

The whole chapter in three sentences

A function of several variables takes several inputs and returns one output, z = f(x, y), and its graph is a surface. To study it, freeze every input except one and do ordinary calculus: that is a partial derivative, the slope of the surface in one direction. Add the partials together with the input changes and you get the total differential dz = fx dx + fy dy, a tangent-plane estimate of how much f changes when all the inputs wiggle at once.

1
Prerequisites and tricks

Toolkit: which rule, and when

Everything in Chapter 13 reuses one-variable derivative rules. For every rule below this section answers the two questions that cause confusion: when do I use it? and where does it show up? Start with the rule finder, then read the tiles: each one lists the exercises that use it and the practice questions that drill it. Every section after this one opens with chips that link back to the rules it needs.

Rule finder: you see → do this

You see… Do this Rule · try
A letter that is not the one you differentiate by Treat it as a number: it stays as a factor, or vanishes if it stands alone. Power · frozen Q13, Q19
Two factors multiplied together Product rule only if both contain your letter. If one is frozen, pull it out. Product Q20, Q35
A fraction Is your letter in the denominator? No: pull the denominator out. Single-term denominator: split into terms. Root: negative power. Otherwise quotient rule. Fraction tricks Q5–10, 25, 26, 52
Something inside e, sin, ln, a power or a root Outside first, copy the inside, multiply by the inside’s derivative (in your letter). Chain Q17, 31–38
ln of a product, quotient or root Split with log laws first, then differentiate each piece. Log laws Q21, 22, 24, 28, 61
cos or cosh cos gets a minus sign, cosh does not. sinh · cosh Q31, 36, 37, 38
√(x² + y²) or ln √(x² + y² + z²) Answer is letter ÷ total: the 2 and the ½ cancel. Radical sum Q29, 59, 61
A letter in the limits of an integral Plug the limit into the integrand: top +, bottom −. Integral limits Q39, 40
“Evaluate at (a, b)” Differentiate with the letters in; substitute last. Evaluate Q45–56, 63–68
“Find the critical points” Set fx = fy = 0, solve together, factor (never divide by a letter), check the domain. Critical pts Q69–76
fxy, ∂²f/∂y∂x, fxyy Differentiate in the order named; mixed partials should match. Higher-order Q77–85, 91–94
A limit as (x, y) → (a, b) Substitute first. 0/0? Test paths y = 0, y = x, y = x². To prove a limit exists, use polar coordinates. Limits 13.2
“Difference quotient” or “limit definition” Expand, cancel, divide by Δx, then let Δx → 0. Roots: conjugate. Δ-quotient 13.1 Q19–20, 13.3 Q41–44
“Is z a function?” or “find the domain” Solve for z (± means no). List the forbidden moves: root ≥ 0, log > 0, denominator ≠ 0. Function test 13.1 Q5–8, Q21–32
w depends on x, y and those depend on t (or on s, t) One product per branch of the tree, then add. Check by substituting first. Multi-chain 13.5
An equation F(x, y) = 0 or F(x, y, z) = 0 defines y or z Differentiate F; the answer is −Fx/Fy (or −Fx/Fz). Implicit 13.5
A direction given as an angle θ, a vector v, or “toward Q” Make a unit vector first (⟨cos θ, sin θ⟩, or v ÷ ‖v‖, or (Q − P) ÷ its length). Unit vector 13.6 Q3–14, 21–28
“Rate of change in the direction of …” Partials at the point, then dot with the unit vector: Duf = ∇f · u. The answer is a number. Directional deriv. 13.6 Q3–14, 21–28
“Steepest”, “fastest increase”, “greatest rate”, “no change”, gradient Gradient = vector of partials. Max rate = its length, direction = the gradient; zero change = perpendicular to it. Gradient 13.6 Q15–20, 29–38
“Relative extrema” or “saddle points” Find critical points (fx = fy = 0 or DNE); test smooth ones with d = fxxfyy − [fxy]2. Second Partials 13.8 Q9, 10, 13–24
“Absolute extrema” on a closed region R Do not use d. Compare f at interior critical points + boundary critical points + corners. Absolute extrema 13.8 Q31–34
“Total differential” dz or dw One term per variable: partial × differential. Total differential 13.4 Q3–8
“Approximate” or “exact Δz and dz” Round base point, partials at the start, dx = new − old (keep the sign). Δz ≈ dz 13.4 Q9–18
A word problem about rates or slopes Say the number with units and direction; compare effects fairly. Units 13.3 Q123, 124

A. Rules from Calculus I that you keep using

Power rule and frozen letters

d/dx (xn) = n xn−1
d/dx (c) = 0
Use whenany term. A letter you are not differentiating by is a plain number: it stays as a factor or vanishes if it stands alone.
Seen in13.3 Q11–16, 25, 29, 30, 58, 77–80
PractiseP17
Drop the power in front, lower it by one. Frozen letters are constants.

Product rule

(uv)′ = u′v + uv′
Use whenboth factors contain the letter you differentiate by. If one factor is frozen, pull it out and skip the product rule (13.3 Q19 and Q34 need none).
Seen in13.3 Q20 and Q35 (y-partials), Q52, Q81
PractiseP9 P13 P14 P15 P19 P23
Keep the first, differentiate the second; then swap.

Quotient rule

uv′ = u′v − uv′v2
Use whenyour letter is in the denominator and you do not want to split or rewrite the fraction. Otherwise see Fraction tricks.
Seen in13.3 Q8–9, 26, 51, 60, 66, 94 · 13.4 Q8
PractiseP11 P12 P19
“Low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared.”

Chain rule

d/dx f(g) = f′(g)·g′
Use whensomething sits inside e, sin, ln, a power or a root. Outside first, copy the inside, then multiply by the derivative of the inside with respect to your letter.
Seen in13.3 Q17–20, 27, 31–38, 47, 57
PractiseP9 P10 P13 P14 P15 P18 P23 P24 P27 P40
Peel the onion: outside first, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.

Exponential and logarithm

(eu)′ = u′eu
(ln u)′ = u′u
Use whenthe function contains e▢ or ln ▢. Differentiate the inside once and keep eu or put u underneath.
Seen in13.3 Q17–23, 27, 28, 35, 45, 46
PractiseP1 P9 P10 P14 P17 P19 P24 P25 P27 P28 P30
eu never changes; ln u puts u underneath.

Trig derivatives

(sin u)′ = u′ cos u
(cos u)′ = −u′ sin u
(tan u)′ = u′ sec2 u
Use whensin, cos or tan of an expression. The inside derivative multiplies the result (chain rule).
Seen in13.3 Q31–36, 47, 48, 57, 83 · 13.4 Q6
PractiseP14 P16 P23 P31
Anything starting with “co” gets a minus sign.

Hyperbolic derivatives

(sinh u)′ = u′ cosh u
(cosh u)′ = u′ sinh u
Use whensinh or cosh. They look like sin and cos but neither derivative has a minus sign.
Seen in13.3 Q37, 38
PractiseP15
Unlike cos, cosh has no minus sign.

Log laws (split first!)

ln(a/b) = ln a − ln b
ln √u = ½ ln u
ln(ab) = ln a + ln b
Use whenln of a product, quotient or root. Break it into separate logs before differentiating: the quotient rule disappears.
Seen in13.3 Q21, 22, 24, 28, 61
PractiseP3 P10 P18 P29
Break the log into pieces before differentiating.

Integral as a function

g = ∫xy h(t) dt
∂g∂y = h(y) , ∂g∂x = −h(x)
Use whena letter appears in the limits of an integral. Plug the limit into the integrand: top limit +, bottom limit −. No need to integrate.
Seen in13.3 Q39, 40 · 13.1 Q17, 18
PractiseP2
Top limit gives +h(top); bottom limit gives −h(bottom).

Domain rules

√u: u ≥ 0
ln u: u > 0
1/u: u ≠ 0
Use whena question asks for the domain, or a critical point could land where the function is undefined.
Seen in13.1 Q21–32 · 13.3 Q73
PractiseP1 P3 P4 P8 P22
Radical ≥ 0, log > 0, denominator ≠ 0.

Boundary curves

x2 + y2 = r2 circle
x2a2 + y2b2 = 1 ellipse
x2a2 − y2b2 = 1 hyperbola
Use whena domain inequality has squares in it: name the edge curve, then test the origin (or another easy point) to choose the side.
Seen in13.1 Q27, 28, 32
PractiseP3 P4
Both squares positive: round. Opposite signs: hyperbola.

Exact trig values

sin(π/6) = ½ , sin(π/4) = √2/2
sin(π/3) = √3/2 , sin(π/2) = 1
cos(π/3) = ½ , cos(π/2) = 0
Use whenyou evaluate a trig partial at a point that includes π. Keep the answer exact (fractions and roots), not a decimal.
Seen in13.3 Q47, 48
PractiseP16
Draw the unit circle once and read the values off.

Difference-quotient algebra

(x+Δx)2 − x2 = 2xΔx + (Δx)2
√a − √b = a − b√a + √b
Use whenthe question says difference quotient or limit definition. Expand, cancel, divide by Δx, then let Δx → 0. Roots: multiply by the conjugate.
Seen in13.1 Q19, 20 · 13.3 Q41–44
PractiseP5
Expand, cancel, divide, then take the limit.

B. New formulas and tricks in Chapter 13

Partial derivative: freeze the rest

fx = limΔx→0 f(x + Δx, y) − f(x, y)Δx
fy = limΔy→0 f(x, y + Δy) − f(x, y)Δy
Use whenevery partial. Say “with respect to x, y is a constant” out loud, then do ordinary one-variable calculus.
Seen in13.3 Q2–44
PractiseP5 P12
Freeze everything except the letter you differentiate by.

Limits in two variables

path test: two paths, two values ⇒ DNE
polar: x = r cosθ, y = r sinθ, and (x, y) → (0, 0) ⇔ r → 0
Use whena limit as (x, y) → (a, b). Substitute first; if you get 0/0, test paths (y = 0, y = x, y = x²); to prove a limit exists switch to polar.
Seen in13.2 limits and continuity
PractiseP6 P7 P8
Different paths, different values: DNE. Same values on a few paths: proves nothing.

Fraction tricks: skip the quotient rule

∂∂x[N(x, y)D(y)] = NxD (D frozen)
Ax + By : term by term
1√u = u−1/2 : chain rule
Use whenyou see a fraction. Ask three questions: is my letter in the denominator? Is the denominator a single term? Is it a root? Often the answer lets you avoid the quotient rule.
Seen in13.3 Q5–10, 25, 52, 62
PractiseP11 P13
Look only at the denominator.

Radical-sum trick

w = √x2 + y2 + z2 ⇒ wx = xw
ln√s = ½ ln s ⇒ xs , s = x2 + y2 + z2
Use when√(x² + y² (+ z²)) or ln of that root. The chain rule’s 2 cancels the ½ and the answer is just letter ÷ total.
Seen in13.3 Q29, 59, 61, 81 · 13.4 Q18
PractiseP18
The ½ and the 2 cancel.

Is it a function?

one z for every (x, y) ⇒ function
z2 = … ⇒ z = ±… ⇒ not a function
Use whena question gives an equation in x, y, z. Solve for z: an even power gives ±, so two outputs, so not a function.
Seen in13.1 Q5–8
PractiseP1
Even power on z means ± means no.

Evaluate at a point

fx(a, b): differentiate first, then x = a, y = b
Use when“evaluate at”, “find the slope at” or “find the rate at” a point. Differentiate with the letters still in; substitute last.
Seen in13.3 Q45–56, 63–68
PractiseP12 P13 P16 P19 P26 P28 P30 P33 P35 P37
Differentiate first, substitute last.

Critical points

fx = 0 and fy = 0, together
Use when“find the critical points”: solve both equations at once by substitution or elimination, factor (never divide by a letter), and check each point is in the domain.
Seen in13.3 Q69–76
PractiseP20 P21 P22
Both partials zero at the same time.

Second, third and mixed partials

fxy = (fx)y : x first, then y
∂²f∂y∂x : same order, written right to left
fxy = fyx (Theorem 13.3)
Use whena subscript list like fxyy or a fraction like ∂²f/∂y∂x. Differentiate in the order named; use equal mixed partials as a free check.
Seen in13.3 Q3–4, 77–85, 91–94
PractiseP17 P23 P24 P25
Subscripts read left to right, the fraction form right to left.

Chain rule: several variables

dw/dt = wx dx/dt + wy dy/dt (+ wz dz/dt)
∂w∂s = wx xs + wy ys
Use whenw depends on x, y (, z), and those depend on t (or on s and t). Write one product per branch of the tree, then add. Substituting x(t), y(t) into w first is a free check.
Seen in13.5 (all chain-rule exercises)
PractiseP30 P31 P34
One product for every branch of the tree.

Implicit differentiation with F

F(x, y) = 0 ⇒ dy/dx = −FxFy
F(x, y, z) = 0 ⇒ ∂z∂x = − FxFz , ∂z∂y = − FyFz
Use whenan equation defines y (or z) implicitly. Move everything to one side as F = 0, find the partials of F, divide, and keep the minus sign.
Seen in13.5 (implicit exercises)
PractiseP32 P33 P38
Minus, then top partial over bottom partial.

Total differential

dz = fx dx + fy dy
dw = wx dx + wy dy + wz dz
Use when“find the total differential”: one term per variable, partial × differential. Leave dx, dy, dz as symbols.
Seen in13.4 Q3–8
PractiseP27
One term for every variable.

Approximation recipe: Δz ≈ dz

Δz ≈ dz = fx(a, b) dx + fy(a, b) dy
dx = new x − old x
Use when“approximate” a messy number or compare exact Δz with dz: choose round base values, evaluate partials at the start, keep the signs of dx and dy.
Seen in13.4 Q9–18
PractiseP28 P29
Partials at the start, signs on the changes.

Rates of change and units

fx ≈ change in f per +1 in x
units: (units of f) per (unit of x)
Use whenthe question is a word problem: say what the number means, with units and direction, and compare effects fairly.
Seen in13.3 Q123, 124
PractiseP26 P34
Number, units, direction.

Making a unit vector (the direction)

u = v/‖v‖
PQ = Q − P (end − start)
u = ⟨cos θ, sin θ⟩
Use whena direction is given as an angle, a vector or “toward Q”. Turn it into a vector of length exactly 1 before using it. Dividing by ‖v‖ is the step everyone forgets.
Seen in13.6 Q3–14, 21–28
PractiseP35 P36 P41
End minus start, then divide by the length.

Directional derivative: slope in any direction

Duf = fx cos θ + fy sin θ
Duf = ∇f · u = a fx + b fy (+ c fz)
Use when“rate of change in the direction of …” (angle, vector or toward Q). Partials at the point, dot them with the unit vector. The answer is a number.
Seen in13.6 Q3–14, 21–28
PractiseP35 P36 P37 P41
Slope east × how much east, plus slope north × how much north.

Gradient, steepest climb and level curves

∇f = ⟨fx, fy, fz⟩
max Duf = ‖∇f‖ (along ∇f) · min = −‖∇f‖
∇f ⟂ level curve
Use when“gradient”, “steepest”, “fastest increase”, “greatest rate”, “no change” or “tangent line to a level curve”. The gradient is a vector; the maximum rate is its length.
Seen in13.6 Q15–20, 29–38
PractiseP37 P38 P39 P40 P41
The gradient points uphill, its length is the steepness, and it is perpendicular to contour lines.

Second Partials Test: relative extrema & saddles

d = fxx(a, b) fyy(a, b) − [fxy(a, b)]2
d > 0, fxx > 0 ⇒ rel. min
d > 0, fxx < 0 ⇒ rel. max
d < 0 ⇒ saddle · d = 0 ⇒ inconclusive
Use whenclassifying smooth critical points (fx = fy = 0). If a partial DNE or d = 0, inspect f(x, y) directly.
Seen in13.8 Q9, 10, 13–24
PractiseP42 P43 P44
d > 0 means same curvature (bowl or dome); d < 0 means a Pringle saddle.

Absolute extrema on a closed bounded region R

1. Interior critical pts inside R
2. Boundary critical pts (1-var g′ = 0)
3. Corner points of R
Use whengiven a closed region R with boundaries. Skip d completely—just plug every candidate into f(x, y) and pick the largest and smallest values.
Seen in13.8 Q31–34
PractiseP45 P46
Extreme Value Theorem: continuous on closed & bounded R guarantees both max and min.

C. Reference: more derivatives, integrals, identities and trig values

More derivatives

(√x)′ = 12√x
(1/x)′ = −1/x2
(ax)′ = ax ln a
(sec u)′ = u′ sec u tan u
(cot u)′ = −u′ csc2 u
(csc u)′ = −u′ csc u cot u
Every “co” function (cos, cot, csc) gets a minus sign.

Integrals you need

∫xn dx = xn+1n + 1 + C (n ≠ −1)
∫1x dx = ln|x| + C
∫ex dx = ex + C
∫sin x dx = −cos x + C
∫cos x dx = sin x + C
∫sec2 x dx = tan x + C
∫ab f dt = F(b) − F(a)
∫yx = −∫xy
Swap the limits, flip the sign (13.1 Q17–18, 13.3 Q39–40).

Identities and log facts

sin2 x + cos2 x = 1
1 + tan2 x = sec2 x
sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x
cos 2x = cos2 x − sin2 x
eln a = a , ln e = 1 , ln 1 = 0
ln(ab) = b ln a
ln 1 = 0 can silently kill a whole term (practice P28).
θ 0 π/6 (30°) π/4 (45°) π/3 (60°) π/2 (90°) π
sin 0 1/2 √2/2 √3/2 1 0
cos 1 √3/2 √2/2 1/2 0 −1
tan 0 1/√3 1 √3 undefined 0

Trick: sin of 0, 30, 45, 60, 90 degrees is √0, √1, √2, √3, √4 all over 2. Cos is the same list backwards.

Write the rule finder on one index card. In an exam, name the variable (“differentiate with respect to x, y is a constant”) and then name the rule before you touch the algebra.

13.1 · Q5–20

Functions of several variables: is it a function, and what is its value?

Toolkit rules for this sectionFunction testIntegral limitsΔ-quotientDomain

A function of two variables z = f(x, y) gives exactly one output z for every input pair (x, y) in its domain. Three-variable functions w = f(x, y, z) work the same way. The slice f(x, y) = c is a level curve, and for three variables f(x, y, z) = c is a level surface. “Evaluate” just means substitute and simplify; the only new habit is that an input can be an expression (like f(x, 4) or h(4, 4t, t2)), and then the answer is an expression too.

Step-by-step method

  1. Is z a function? Solve the equation for z. One expression for z = function. A “±” (or an even power of z you cannot undo) = not a function.
  2. Evaluate. Write the rule with empty slots, then put each input in brackets into its slot. Simplify last.
  3. Integral-defined functions. Integrate first: ∫xy h(t) dt = H(y) − H(x), then substitute.
  4. Difference quotients. Replace only the variable that moves (x → x + Δx or y → y + Δy), expand, subtract f(x, y), divide by the increment.

Question types

Exercises What it asks Key move
Q5–8 Is z a function of x and y? Solve for z; look for ±
Q9–16 Evaluate at numbers or expressions Substitute in brackets, simplify
Q17–18 Function defined by an integral Antiderivative, top minus bottom
Q19–20 Difference quotients in x and in y Expand, cancel, divide

In a difference quotient, f(x + Δx, y) changes only x. Students also add Δx to y and then lose the cancellation. Also: (x + Δx)2 ≠ x2 + (Δx)2; the middle term 2xΔx is the one that survives.

Worked examples

EasySubstituting into f(x, y) = 2x − y + 3Q9 (d)(e)(f)
Question

For f(x, y) = 2x − y + 3, find f(3, y), f(x, 4) and f(5, t).

  1. f(3, y): replace x by 3 and keep y: 2(3) − y + 3 = 6 − y + 3.
  2. f(x, 4): replace y by 4 and keep x: 2x − 4 + 3 = 2x − 1.
  3. f(5, t): 2(5) − t + 3 = 13 − t.
f(3, y) = 9 − y  ·  f(x, 4) = 2x − 1  ·  f(5, t) = 13 − t
MediumIs z a function of x and y?Q8 (and Q5–7)
Question

Decide whether z + x ln y − 8yz = 0 defines z as a function of x and y.

  1. Collect the z-terms: z − 8yz = −x ln y, so z(1 − 8y) = −x ln y.
  2. Divide: z = −x ln y1 − 8y = x ln y8y − 1 .
  3. For every allowed pair there is one z, with no ± anywhere. The formula needs y > 0 (for ln y) and y ≠ 18.
Yes, z is a function of x and y (domain: y > 0, y ≠ 18 ).
MediumTwo values of z for one point: not a functionQ6, Q7
Question

Test xz2 + 2xy − y2 = 4 and x24 + y29 + z2 = 1 .

  1. Q6: xz2 = 4 − 2xy + y2 gives z = ±√ 4 − 2xy + y2x .
  2. Pick (x, y) = (1, 0): z2 = 4 so z = 2 and z = −2. Two outputs for one input.
  3. Q7 (an ellipsoid): z = ±√1 − x24 − y29 . At (0, 0): z = ±1.
Q6 and Q7 are not functions of x and y. Q5 and Q8 are.
HardA function defined by an integralQ17 (c)
Question

g(x, y) = ∫xy (2t − 3) dt. Find g(4, 32).

  1. Antiderivative of 2t − 3 is t2 − 3t.
  2. g(x, y) = [t2 − 3t]xy = (y2 − 3y) − (x2 − 3x).
  3. Substitute x = 4, y = 32: top: 94 − 92 = −94 ; bottom: 16 − 12 = 4.
  4. Top minus bottom: −94 − 4 = −254 .
g(4, 32) = −254
HardDifference quotientsQ20 (and Q19)
Question

f(x, y) = 3x2 − 2y. Simplify f(x + Δx, y) − f(x, y)Δx and f(x, y + Δy) − f(x, y)Δy .

  1. (a) f(x + Δx, y) = 3(x + Δx)2 − 2y = 3x2 + 6xΔx + 3(Δx)2 − 2y.
  2. Subtract f(x, y): left with 6xΔx + 3(Δx)2. Divide by Δx: 6x + 3Δx.
  3. (b) f(x, y + Δy) = 3x2 − 2y − 2Δy. Subtract f(x, y): −2Δy. Divide by Δy: −2.
  4. Check: letting Δ→0 gives 6x and −2, the partial derivatives fx, fy. That is exactly what the quotient is for.
(a) 6x + 3Δx  ·  (b) −2
Answer bank · Q5–Q19 (everything not worked above)

13.1 · Q21–32

Domain and range

Toolkit rules for this sectionDomainBoundaryLog laws

The domain is the set of all (x, y) where the formula makes sense; the range is the set of values z can take. Domain = list the “forbidden moves” (divide by 0, root of a negative, log of a non-positive) and describe what is left as a region of the xy-plane.

Step-by-step method

  1. List every restriction in the formula: denominators, even roots, logs.
  2. Turn each into an inequality in x and y, for example 4 − x2 − y2 ≥ 0.
  3. Identify the boundary curve (circle, line, hyperbola…) and test the origin or another easy point to see which side is allowed.
  4. State it in words and symbols: “all points on or inside the circle…”, “all points with xy > 6”.
  5. Range: find the smallest and largest value of the inside expression, then push that interval through the outer function.

Question types

Exercises Shape of the formula Domain turns out to be
Q21, Q22 Polynomial, exponential Whole plane ℝ2
Q23, Q24 Root times/over something Half-plane (y ≥ 0 or x > 0)
Q25, Q26 Rational function Plane minus a line or two
Q27, Q28 Square root of a quadratic Disk, or region between hyperbola branches
Q31, Q32 Natural log Half-plane x + y < 5, or xy > 6 (two curved regions)

Range shortcut: pick a path where the inside expression moves through all its values (e.g. set y = 0 or x = y) and see what outputs you get. If you can reach every number in an interval, that interval is in the range.

Closed or open boundary? A square root allows 0, so its boundary curve is included (≥, Q27, Q28). A log or a denominator cannot be 0 (or negative), so its boundary is excluded (>, ≠, Q24, Q31, Q32).

Worked examples

EasyExponential: no restrictionsQ22
Question

Find the domain and range of f(x, y) = exy.

  1. e to any real power is defined, and xy is defined for every pair. No restriction.
  2. Range: eu is always positive. Can xy take every real value? Yes (choose y = 1, x anything), so exy takes every positive value.
Domain: all (x, y) (the whole plane). Range: (0, ∞), i.e. z > 0.
MediumSquare root of a quadraticQ27
Question

f(x, y) = √4 − x2 − y2.

  1. Radicand ≥ 0: 4 − x2 − y2 ≥ 0 ⇒ x2 + y2 ≤ 4.
  2. That is the closed disk of radius 2 centred at the origin (boundary included because of ≥).
  3. Range: the radicand goes from 0 (on the circle) up to 4 (at the origin), so z = √(radicand) goes from 0 to 2.
Domain: x2 + y2 ≤ 4. Range: [0, 2] (the graph is the upper half of a sphere of radius 2).
HardA hyperbola-bounded regionQ28
Question

f(x, y) = √9 − 6x2 + y2.

  1. Radicand ≥ 0: 9 − 6x2 + y2 ≥ 0 ⇒ 6x2 − y2 ≤ 9.
  2. Boundary 6x2 − y2 = 9, i.e. x23/2 − y29 = 1 : a hyperbola opening left and right, vertices (±√3/2, 0).
  3. Test the origin: 0 ≤ 9 is true, so the origin is allowed. The allowed region is the part between and including the two branches (it contains the whole y-axis).
  4. Range: on the y-axis f(0, y) = √9 + y2 covers [3, ∞); moving toward a vertex shrinks the radicand to 0. So every value ≥ 0 occurs.
Domain: 6x2 − y2 ≤ 9. Range: [0, ∞).
HardLog of a product: region between curvesQ32
Question

f(x, y) = ln(xy − 6).

  1. A log needs a positive inside: xy − 6 > 0 ⇒ xy > 6.
  2. Boundary xy = 6 is a hyperbola with one branch in quadrant I and one in quadrant III (it never touches the axes). Test (3, 3): 9 > 6 ✓, so the allowed region is the part above and to the right of the quadrant I branch and below and to the left of the quadrant III branch. The curve itself is excluded (strict >).
  3. Range: xy − 6 takes every positive value (take y = 1, x > 6 anything), and ln of every positive number gives every real number.
Domain: {(x, y): xy > 6}. Range: (−∞, ∞).

Q24
g = y√x: domain x > 0 (strict, root is in the denominator), y any; range all reals.
Q25
z = x + yxy: domain x ≠ 0 and y ≠ 0 (both axes removed); range all reals (z = 1/x + 1/y; x = −y gives 0, x = y = t gives 2/t).

z = xyx + y: domain x + y ≠ 0 (line y = −x removed); range all reals (x = y = t gives t/2).

Q31

13.2

Limits and continuity: do all paths agree?

Toolkit rules for this sectionLimitsDomain

The key difference from one variable. In one variable you approach a point from two sides. In two variables you can approach from infinitely many paths. A limit exists only if every path gives the same value, so a single pair of different values is enough to show it does not exist.

Step-by-step method

  1. Try substitution first. If the function is defined at the point (polynomials, e▢, sin, cos, fractions whose denominator is not 0 there), plug in and you are done.
  2. Got 0/0 at (0, 0)? Test two paths: y = 0 and y = x. Different values ⇒ the limit does not exist (DNE).
  3. Same value on those paths proves nothing. Try a curved path (for example y = x2), or prove the limit with polar coordinates: x = r cosθ, y = r sinθ, and (x, y) → (0, 0) becomes r → 0. If the result is r times something bounded, the limit is 0.
  4. Continuity at a point needs three things: f is defined there, the limit exists, and the two are equal.

Question types

Type Method Watch for
Limit of a nice function Substitute the point Check the denominator is not 0
0/0 at (0, 0): does it exist? Paths y = 0, y = x, then a curve Two different values ⇒ DNE
Prove a limit equals 0 Polar coordinates and a squeeze Bounded factor: |cosθ|, |sinθ| ≤ 1
Where is f continuous? Rational: wherever the denominator ≠ 0 Removable (limit exists) or not

Straight lines can all agree and still be wrong. x2y/(x4 + y2) gives 0 along every line y = mx, but ½ along the parabola y = x2. When lines agree, try one curved path before you claim the limit exists (practice P6).

Pick the path that makes the denominator collapse: if you see x4 + y2 try y = x2; if you see x2 + y2 try lines and polar.

Worked examples

EasySubstitute13.2
Question

Evaluate (a) lim(x, y)→(3, 1) x2 − 2y (b) lim(x, y)→(1, 2) exy (c) lim(x, y)→(0, 2) x/y.

  1. Each function is defined and continuous at its point (the denominator in (c) is y = 2 ≠ 0), so substitute.
  2. (a) 32 − 2·1 = 7. (b) e1·2 = e2. (c) 0/2 = 0.
7, e2, 0
Medium0/0: two paths, two values13.2
Question

Does lim(x, y)→(0, 0) xyx2 + y2 exist?

  1. Substituting gives 0/0, so test paths.
  2. Along y = 0: x·0x2 + 0 = 0.
  3. Along y = x: x2x2 + x2 = x22x2 = ½ .
  4. Two different values, so no single limit.
The limit does not exist.
HardProve a limit with polar coordinates13.2
Question

Find lim(x, y)→(0, 0) xy2x2 + y2 .

  1. Both paths y = 0 and y = x give 0, but that is not a proof. Switch to polar: x = r cosθ, y = r sinθ.
  2. r cosθ · r2 sin2θr2 = r cosθ sin2θ .
  3. Since |cosθ sin2θ| ≤ 1, the expression is squeezed between −r and r, and r → 0.
The limit is 0.
MediumContinuity: where, and is it removable?13.2
Question

(a) Where is f(x, y) = 2y − x2 continuous? (b) Is the discontinuity of g(x, y) = x2 − y2x − y removable?

  1. (a) A rational function is continuous wherever its denominator is not 0. y − x2 = 0 is the parabola y = x2. Near it |f| blows up, so there is no limit: a nonremovable discontinuity.
  2. (b) g is undefined on the line y = x. For x ≠ y, g = (x − y)(x + y)x − y = x + y, so at a point (a, a) the limit is 2a.
  3. The limit exists, so the discontinuity is removable: define g(x, x) = 2x and g becomes continuous.
(a) Discontinuous exactly on y = x2 (nonremovable). (b) Removable along y = x.

13.3 · Q2–44

Partial derivatives: first-order, rules and the limit definition

Toolkit rules for this sectionPartial defPower · frozenProductQuotientFraction tricksChaine · lnLog lawsTrigsinh · coshIntegral limitsΔ-quotient

A partial derivative ∂f∂x is the ordinary derivative of f with respect to x while every other variable is frozen as a constant. Geometrically it is the slope of the surface in the x-direction (the slope of the trace you get by cutting the surface with the plane y = y0); ∂f∂y is the slope in the y-direction.

Notation, all the same thing: ∂z∂x = ∂f/∂x = fx(x, y) = zx = Dxf .

Step-by-step method

  1. Name the variable. Say it out loud: “with respect to x; y is a constant”. Mentally replace the frozen letters with numbers.
  2. Pick the rule exactly as in one variable: power, product, quotient, chain.
  3. Chain rule: derivative of the outside × the partial of the inside with respect to the same variable.
  4. Repeat for the other variable. Any term that does not contain your variable differentiates to 0.
  5. Limit-definition exercises (Q41–44): fx = limΔx→0 f(x + Δx, y) − f(x, y)Δx , and the same with Δy for fy.

Question types

Exercises Type What to watch
Q2–4 Concept check Notation, geometry, order of mixed derivatives
Q5–10 Quotient rule or not? Is the variable in the denominator?
Q11–16, Q29, Q30 Polynomials and roots Rewrite roots as powers
Q17–20, Q27 Exponentials Chain rule on the exponent
Q21–24, Q28 Logarithms Split the log first
Q25, Q26 Rational functions Term-by-term or quotient rule
Q31–38 Trig and hyperbolic Chain rule, product rule
Q39, Q40 Integral-defined Top limit +, bottom limit −
Q41–44 Limit definition Expand, cancel, then take the limit

Quotient-rule test (Q5–10): look only at the denominator. If it contains the variable you are differentiating with respect to, use the quotient rule. If it does not, the denominator is a constant: just pull it out and differentiate the numerator.

Differentiating a frozen letter. In ∂∂x(x2y) the y is a constant, so the answer is 2xy, not 2xy + x2 (that extra x2 comes from wrongly differentiating y). The other trap: z = ln√xy looks like a chain-rule monster, but ln√xy = ½ln x + ½ln y makes it trivial.

Worked examples

EasyPolynomial in two variablesQ13
Question

Find both first partial derivatives zx and zy of z = −x2y + 6x + 8y2.

Think firstBefore any algebra, name the shape. It is a sum. Terms can be handled one at a time, and any term that does not contain the letter you are differentiating by is a constant, so it dies (becomes 0). Then do the x-partial with y frozen, and the y-partial with x frozen.
1

We differentiate with respect to x. That means y is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while x is the only thing allowed to move.

zx= ∂∂x[−x2y + 6x + 8y2]

Whythe partial derivative zx asks: how fast does z change when only x changes?

2

This is a sum, so differentiate each term separately and add the answers.

∂∂x[6x] =6·1 ∂∂x[8y2] =0 ∂∂x[−x2y] =(−y)·[2·x]total=6 + 0 + −2xy=−2xy + 6

Whythe sum rule says the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. Going term by term: term 1 (6x): 6 has no x, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of x with respect to x is 1; term 2 (8y2): there is no x anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as x is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0; term 3 (−x2y): −y has no x, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then power rule: bring the exponent down in front, then lower the exponent by 1.

3

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

zy= ∂∂y[−x2y + 6x + 8y2]
4

This is a sum, so differentiate each term separately and add the answers.

∂∂y[6x] =0 ∂∂y[8y2] =8·[2·y] ∂∂y[−x2y] =(−x2)·1total=0 + 16y + −x2=−x2 + 16y

Whythe sum rule says the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. Going term by term: term 1 (6x): there is no y anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as y is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0; term 2 (8y2): 8 has no y, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then power rule: bring the exponent down in front, then lower the exponent by 1; term 3 (−x2y): −x2 has no y, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of y with respect to y is 1.

zx = −2xy + 6  ·  zy = −x2 + 16y
MediumProduct and chain rule togetherQ20
Question

Find both first partial derivatives zx and zy of z = 7yey/x.

Think firstBefore any algebra, name the shape. Everything except one piece is frozen, so you are really differentiating a constant × one piece. The constant just rides along. Then do the x-partial with y frozen, and the y-partial with x frozen.
1

We differentiate with respect to x. That means y is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while x is the only thing allowed to move.

zx= ∂∂x[7yey/x]

Whythe partial derivative zx asks: how fast does z change when only x changes?

2

7y has no x in it, so it is just a number sitting in front. Numbers ride along untouched; we only differentiate the part that moves: ey/x.

∂∂x[7yey/x] =7y·∂∂x[ey/x]

Whythe constant multiple rule: (c·g)′ = c·g′.

3

This is a function inside a function: e to the power of something. The outside is e□ and the inside is yx . That means the chain rule.

outside=e□inside g= yx

Whythe chain rule in words: "derivative of the outside (leave the inside alone), times the derivative of the inside".

4

Differentiate the inside, yx , with respect to x.

∂∂x[ yx] = 0·x − y·1x2 =− yx2

Why yx : quotient rule: (u′w − uw′) over w².

5

Multiply: (derivative of the outside, inside untouched) × (derivative of the inside).

∂∂x[ey/x] =ey/x·(−yx2 )=− yey/xx2
6

Bring the constant multiplier back in.

∂∂x[7yey/x] =7y·(− yey/xx2)=−7y2ey/xx2
7

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

zy= ∂∂y[7yey/x]
8

7 has no y, so it rides along. y and ey/x are multiplied together and both contain y. That is a job for the product rule.

u=yw=ey/x
∂∂y[u·w] = u′·w + u·w′

Whyboth factors are changing, so each one gets a turn: "derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times the derivative of the second".

9

Differentiate each factor on its own, as if the other was not there.

u′=1w′=ey/x·1x = ey/xx

Whyfor u: the derivative of y with respect to y is 1. For w: e( ) copies itself, and the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of the exponent.

10

Drop the pieces into the product rule u′w + uw′ and tidy up.

∂∂y[7yey/x] =7[1·ey/x + y· ey/xx]= 7(x + y)ey/xx
zx = − 7y2ey/xx2  ·  zy = 7(x + y)ey/xx
MediumSplit the log before you differentiateQ24
Question

Find both first partial derivatives zx and zy of z = ln(x + yx − y).

Think firstBefore any algebra, name the shape. ln of something: the answer is 1 over the inside, times the derivative of the inside. Always ask first whether a log law can split it. Then do the x-partial with y frozen, and the y-partial with x frozen.
1

Use the log law ln(a/b) = ln a − ln b first.

z=ln(x + yx − y)=−ln(x − y) + ln(x + y)

Whynow there is no quotient rule at all, only two small chain rules.

2

We differentiate with respect to x. That means y is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while x is the only thing allowed to move.

zx= ∂∂x[−ln(x − y) + ln(x + y)]

Whythe partial derivative zx asks: how fast does z change when only x changes?

3

This is a sum, so differentiate each term separately and add the answers.

∂∂x[−ln(x − y)] =(−1)·[1x − y] ∂∂x[ln(x + y)] = 1x + y total=−1x − y + 1x + y=−2y(x − y)(x + y)

Whythe sum rule says the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. Going term by term: term 1 (−ln(x − y)): −1 has no x, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then ln( ) turns into 1 over the inside, and the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of the inside; term 2 (ln(x + y)): ln( ) turns into 1 over the inside, and the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of the inside.

4

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

zy= ∂∂y[−ln(x − y) + ln(x + y)]
5

This is a sum, so differentiate each term separately and add the answers.

∂∂y[−ln(x − y)] =(−1)·[(−1)x − y] ∂∂y[ln(x + y)] = 1x + y total= 1x − y + 1x + y = 2x(x − y)(x + y)

Whythe sum rule says the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. Going term by term: term 1 (−ln(x − y)): −1 has no y, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then ln( ) turns into 1 over the inside, and the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of the inside; term 2 (ln(x + y)): ln( ) turns into 1 over the inside, and the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of the inside.

6

Tidy up: the same two answers written in the neatest form (the usual textbook form).

zx=− 2y(x − y)(x + y)=−2yx2 − y2zy= 2x(x − y)(x + y) = 2xx2 − y2

Whyfactoring or combining fractions makes the answer shorter and easier to check, and it matches how the answer key usually looks.

zx = −2yx2 − y2  ·  zy = 2xx2 − y2
HardQuotient rule in a symmetric fractionQ26
Question

Find both first partial derivatives zx and zy of z = xyx2 + y2.

Think firstBefore any algebra, name the shape. The letter appears on the bottom (or both), so the quotient rule comes in: (top′·bottom − top·bottom′) ÷ bottom². Then do the x-partial with y frozen, and the y-partial with x frozen.
1

We differentiate with respect to x. That means y is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while x is the only thing allowed to move.

zx= ∂∂x[ xyx2 + y2]

Whythe partial derivative zx asks: how fast does z change when only x changes?

2

A fraction whose bottom contains x: that is the quotient rule. Call the top u and the bottom w.

u=xyw=x2 + y2
∂∂x[ uw] = u′·w − u·w′w2

Whythe rhyme: "low d-high minus high d-low, over the square of what's below". Keep the order, because the minus sign makes it matter.

3

Differentiate the top and the bottom separately.

u′=y·1=yw′=2·x + 0=2x

Whytop: y has no x, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of x with respect to x is 1. Bottom: sum rule: differentiate each term on its own.

4

Put the pieces into the quotient rule and clean up.

∂∂x[ xyx2 + y2] = y·(x2 + y2) − xy·2x(x2 + y2)2 = y(−x2 + y2)(x2 + y2)2
5

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

zy= ∂∂y[ xyx2 + y2]
6

A fraction whose bottom contains y: that is the quotient rule. Call the top u and the bottom w.

u=xyw=x2 + y2
∂∂y[ uw] = u′·w − u·w′w2

Whythe rhyme: "low d-high minus high d-low, over the square of what's below". Keep the order, because the minus sign makes it matter.

7

Differentiate the top and the bottom separately.

u′=x·1=xw′=0 + 2·y=2y

Whytop: x has no y, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of y with respect to y is 1. Bottom: sum rule: differentiate each term on its own.

8

Put the pieces into the quotient rule and clean up.

∂∂y[ xyx2 + y2] = x·(x2 + y2) − xy·2y(x2 + y2)2 = x(x2 − y2)(x2 + y2)2
zx = y(−x2 + y2)(x2 + y2)2  ·  zy = x(x2 − y2)(x2 + y2)2

Tap a question to open its full solution.
Q1–Q4 · concept check
Q1Notation
Question

Write three other ways to denote the partial derivative of z = f(x, y) with respect to x.

Think firstThis is just vocabulary: same object, different handwriting.
1

Recall that a partial derivative can be written in several equivalent ways.

= ∂z∂x =fx(x, y)=zx=∂f/∂x=Dxf

Whythe curly ∂ (not a normal d) tells you more than one letter is present, and everything else is frozen. The subscript x says which letter moves.

Any three of: ∂z∂x , fx(x, y), zx, ∂f/∂x, Dxf.
Q2Geometric meaning
Question

Describe the geometric meaning of the partial derivatives of z = f(x, y).

Think firstDraw a hill. Which way are you walking, and what is staying frozen?
1

Picture the surface as a hillside and stand on one point.

Whyevery partial derivative is a slope; we only need to say which direction we walk.

2

Walk in the direction of increasing x, keeping y fixed. The slope of the ground under your feet is ∂f∂x .

Whycutting the hillside with the plane y = y0 leaves a curve (a 'trace'), and ∂f∂x is the slope of that curve.

3

Walk in the direction of increasing y, keeping x fixed: that slope is ∂f∂y .

∂f∂x = slope of the surface in the x-direction; ∂f∂y = slope in the y-direction.
Q3Order of mixed partials
Question

Explain the difference between fyxz and ∂²f∂x∂z .

Think firstWhich notation reads left-to-right and which right-to-left?
1

Read the subscript version left to right: fyxz means first y, then x, then z.

Whyin subscript notation the letters are listed in the order the derivatives are taken.

2

Read the fraction version right to left: ∂²f∂x∂z means first z, then x.

Whythe symbol ∂²f/∂x∂z has the innermost derivative (the one acting on f first) on the right.

(a) fyxz: y, then x, then z. (b) ∂²f∂x∂z : z, then x.
Q4Mixed partials commute
Question

Is it true that fxy = fyx for a nice function?

Think firstDoes the order matter?
1

Recall Clairaut's theorem (Theorem 13.3).

Whyit says the order of differentiation does not matter, as long as both mixed partials are continuous on an open region.

2

Almost every function in this chapter (polynomials, exponentials, trig) is continuous everywhere it is defined, so the condition holds.

Watch outUse this as a free check: compute both mixed partials and they must agree.

Yes: fxy = fyx when both are continuous on an open disk.
Q5–Q10 · should the quotient rule be used?
Q5No · ∂∂x(x2yy2 − 3)
Question

Differentiate f(x, y) = x2yy2 − 3 with respect to x. Is the quotient rule needed?

Think firstOnly one question matters: does the bottom contain the letter I am differentiating by?
1

Look only at the bottom: y2 − 3. Does it contain x?

bottom=y2 − 3contains x?=no, so it is a constant

Whywe are differentiating with respect to x, and y is frozen. A bottom with no x is just a number (like 4 or 7), and a number in the denominator can be pulled out front.

Watch outNo quotient rule. Treat the fraction as (1 ÷ constant) × top.

2

We differentiate with respect to x. That means y is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while x is the only thing allowed to move.

fx= ∂∂x[ x2yy2 − 3]

Whythe partial derivative fx asks: how fast does f change when only x changes?

3

yy2 − 3 has no x in it, so it rides along as a multiplier, and only x2 is differentiated.

∂∂x[ x2yy2 − 3] = yy2 − 3·[2·x] = 2xyy2 − 3

Why yy2 − 3 has no x, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then power rule: bring the exponent down in front, then lower the exponent by 1

No quotient rule needed. fx = 2xyy2 − 3
Q6Yes · ∂∂y(x2yy2 − 3)
Question

Differentiate f(x, y) = x2yy2 − 3 with respect to y. Is the quotient rule needed?

Think firstOnly one question matters: does the bottom contain the letter I am differentiating by?
1

Look only at the bottom: y2 − 3. Does it contain y?

bottom=y2 − 3contains y?=yes, it moves

Whythe bottom changes when y changes, so we cannot pull it out. We need the quotient rule.

Watch outThe word 'yes' on this test means: top′·bottom − top·bottom′, all over bottom².

2

We differentiate with respect to y. That means x is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while y is the only thing allowed to move.

fy= ∂∂y[ x2yy2 − 3]

Whythe partial derivative fy asks: how fast does f change when only y changes?

3

A fraction whose bottom contains y: that is the quotient rule. Call the top u and the bottom w.

u=x2yw=y2 − 3
∂∂y[ uw] = u′·w − u·w′w2

Whythe rhyme: "low d-high minus high d-low, over the square of what's below". Keep the order, because the minus sign makes it matter.

4

Differentiate the top and the bottom separately.

u′=x2·1=x2w′=0 + 2·y=2y

Whytop: x2 has no y, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of y with respect to y is 1. Bottom: sum rule: differentiate each term on its own.

5

Put the pieces into the quotient rule and clean up.

∂∂y[ x2yy2 − 3] = x2·(y2 − 3) − x2y·2y(y2 − 3)2 = x2(−y2 − 3)y4 − 6y2 + 9
Quotient rule needed. fy = x2(−y2 − 3)y4 − 6y2 + 9
Q7No · ∂∂y(x − yx2 + 1)
Question

Differentiate f(x, y) = x − yx2 + 1 with respect to y. Is the quotient rule needed?

Think firstOnly one question matters: does the bottom contain the letter I am differentiating by?
1

Look only at the bottom: x2 + 1. Does it contain y?

bottom=x2 + 1contains y?=no, so it is a constant

Whywe are differentiating with respect to y, and x is frozen. A bottom with no y is just a number (like 4 or 7), and a number in the denominator can be pulled out front.

Watch outNo quotient rule. Treat the fraction as (1 ÷ constant) × top.

2

We differentiate with respect to y. That means x is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while y is the only thing allowed to move.

fy= ∂∂y[ x − yx2 + 1]

Whythe partial derivative fy asks: how fast does f change when only y changes?

3

1x2 + 1 has no y in it, so it rides along as a multiplier, and only x − y is differentiated.

∂∂y[ x − yx2 + 1] = 1x2 + 1·[0 + (−1)·1] =− 1x2 + 1

Why 1x2 + 1 has no y, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then sum rule: differentiate each term on its own

No quotient rule needed. fy = −1x2 + 1

2

Whythe partial derivative fx asks: how fast does f change when only x changes?

3

A fraction whose bottom contains x: that is the quotient rule. Call the top u and the bottom w.

u=x − yw=x2 + 1
∂∂x[ uw] = u′·w − u·w′w2

Whythe rhyme: "low d-high minus high d-low, over the square of what's below". Keep the order, because the minus sign makes it matter.

4

Differentiate the top and the bottom separately.

u′=1 + 0=1w′=0 + 2·x=2x

Q11–Q38 · first partials
Q11f = 2x − 5y + 3
Question

Find both first partial derivatives fx and fy of f(x, y) = 2x − 5y + 3.

Think firstBefore any algebra, name the shape. It is a sum. Terms can be handled one at a time, and any term that does not contain the letter you are differentiating by is a constant, so it dies (becomes 0). Then do the x-partial with y frozen, and the y-partial with x frozen.
1

We differentiate with respect to x. That means y is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while x is the only thing allowed to move.

fx= ∂∂x[2x − 5y + 3]

Whythe partial derivative fx asks: how fast does f change when only x changes?

2

This is a sum, so differentiate each term separately and add the answers.

∂∂x[3] =0 ∂∂x[−5y] =0 ∂∂x[2x] =2·1total=0 + 0 + 2 = 2

Whythe sum rule says the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. Going term by term: term 1 (3): there is no x anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as x is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0; term 2 (−5y): there is no x anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as x is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0; term 3 (2x): 2 has no x, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of x with respect to x is 1.

3

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

fy= ∂∂y[2x − 5y + 3]
4

This is a sum, so differentiate each term separately and add the answers.

∂∂y[3] =0 ∂∂y[−5y] =(−5)·1 ∂∂y[2x] =0total=0 + −5 + 0 = −5

Whythe sum rule says the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. Going term by term: term 1 (3): there is no y anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as y is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0; term 2 (−5y): −5 has no y, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of y with respect to y is 1; term 3 (2x): there is no y anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as y is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0.

fx = 2  ·  fy = −5

fx= ∂∂x[x2 − 2y2 + 4]

Whythe partial derivative fx asks: how fast does f change when only x changes?

2

This is a sum, so differentiate each term separately and add the answers.

∂∂x[4] =0 ∂∂x[x2] =2·x ∂∂x[−2y2] =0total=0 + 2x + 0 = 2x

Whythe sum rule says the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. Going term by term: term 1 (4): there is no x anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as x is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0; term 2 (x2): power rule: bring the exponent down in front, then lower the exponent by 1; term 3 (−2y2): there is no x anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as x is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0.

3

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

fy= ∂∂y[x2 − 2y2 + 4]

Going term by term: term 1 (4): there is no y anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as y is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0; term 2 (x2): there is no y anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as y is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0; term 3 (−2y2): −2 has no y, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then power rule: bring the exponent down in front, then lower the exponent by 1.

fx = 2x  ·  fy = −4y
Q13z = −x2y + 6x + 8y2
Question

1

We differentiate with respect to x. That means y is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while x is the only thing allowed to move.

zx= ∂∂x[−x2y + 6x + 8y2]

Whythe partial derivative zx asks: how fast does z change when only x changes?

2

This is a sum, so differentiate each term separately and add the answers.

∂∂x[6x] =6·1 ∂∂x[8y2] =0 ∂∂x[−x2y] =(−y)·[2·x]total=6 + 0 + −2xy=−2xy + 6

Whythe sum rule says the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives. Going term by term: term 1 (6x): 6 has no x, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of x with respect to x is 1; term 2 (8y2): there is no x anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as x is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0; term 3 (−x2y): −y has no x, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then power rule: bring the exponent down in front, then lower the exponent by 1.

zx = −2xy + 6  ·  zy = −x2 + 16y
Q14f = 4x3y2
Question

Find both first partial derivatives fx and fy of f(x, y) = 4x3y2.

Think firstBefore any algebra, name the shape. Everything except one piece is frozen, so you are really differentiating a constant × one piece. The constant just rides along. Then do the x-partial with y frozen, and the y-partial with x frozen.
1

We differentiate with respect to x. That means y is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while x is the only thing allowed to move.

fx= ∂∂x[ 4x3y2]

Whythe partial derivative fx asks: how fast does f change when only x changes?

2

4y2 has no x in it, so it rides along as a multiplier, and only x3 is differentiated.

∂∂x[ 4x3y2] = 4y2·[3·x2] = 12x2y2

Why 4y2 has no x, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then power rule: bring the exponent down in front, then lower the exponent by 1

3

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

fy= ∂∂y[ 4x3y2]
4

A fraction whose bottom contains y: that is the quotient rule. Call the top u and the bottom w. The top, 4x3, has no y, so u′ = 0 and the rule shrinks to −u·w′ / w².

u=4x3w=y2
∂∂y[ uw] = u′·w − u·w′w2

Whythe rhyme: "low d-high minus high d-low, over the square of what's below". Keep the order, because the minus sign makes it matter.

5

Differentiate the top and the bottom separately.

u′=0w′=2·y=2y

Whytop: there is no y anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as y is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0. Bottom: power rule: bring the exponent down in front, then lower the exponent by 1.

6

Put the pieces into the quotient rule and clean up.

∂∂y[ 4x3y2] = 0·y2 − 4x3·2y(y2)2 =− 8x3y3
fx = 12x2y2  ·  fy = −8x3y3

Q17z = exy
Question

Find both first partial derivatives zx and zy of z = exy.

Think firstBefore any algebra, name the shape. e to something: the e… stays exactly as it is, and we multiply by the derivative of the exponent (chain rule). Then do the x-partial with y frozen, and the y-partial with x frozen.
1

We differentiate with respect to x. That means y is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while x is the only thing allowed to move.

zx= ∂∂x[exy]

Whythe partial derivative zx asks: how fast does z change when only x changes?

2

This is a function inside a function: e to the power of something. The outside is e□ and the inside is xy. That means the chain rule.

outside=e□inside g=xy

Whythe chain rule in words: "derivative of the outside (leave the inside alone), times the derivative of the inside".

3

Differentiate the inside, xy, with respect to x.

∂∂x[xy] =y·1=y

Whyxy: y has no x, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of x with respect to x is 1.

4

Multiply: (derivative of the outside, inside untouched) × (derivative of the inside).

∂∂x[exy] =exy·y=yexy
5

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

zy= ∂∂y[exy]
6

This is a function inside a function: e to the power of something. The outside is e□ and the inside is xy. That means the chain rule.

outside=e□inside g=xy

Whythe chain rule in words: "derivative of the outside (leave the inside alone), times the derivative of the inside".

7

Differentiate the inside, xy, with respect to y.

∂∂y[xy] =x·1=x

Whyxy: x has no y, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of y with respect to y is 1.

8

Multiply: (derivative of the outside, inside untouched) × (derivative of the inside).

∂∂y[exy] =exy·x=xexy
zx = yexy  ·  zy = xexy

Think firstBefore any algebra, name the shape. Everything except one piece is frozen, so you are really differentiating a constant × one piece. The constant just rides along. Then do the x-partial with y frozen, and the y-partial with x frozen.

This is a function inside a function: e to the power of something. The outside is e□ and the inside is yx . That means the chain rule.

outside=e□inside g= yx

Question

Find both first partial derivatives zx and zy of z = ln(xy).

Multiply: (derivative of the outside, inside untouched) × (derivative of the inside).

∂∂y[cos(xy)] =−sin(xy)·x=−x sin(xy)
zx = −y sin(xy)  ·  zy = −x sin(xy)
Q32z = sin(x + 2y)
Question

Find both first partial derivatives zx and zy of z = sin(x + 2y).

Think firstBefore any algebra, name the shape. A trig function of something: use the derivative of the trig function, copy the inside unchanged, then multiply by the derivative of the inside. Then do the x-partial with y frozen, and the y-partial with x frozen.
1

We differentiate with respect to x. That means y is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while x is the only thing allowed to move.

zx= ∂∂x[sin(x + 2y)]

Whythe partial derivative zx asks: how fast does z change when only x changes?

2

This is a function inside a function: sin of something. The outside is sin(□) and the inside is x + 2y. That means the chain rule.

outside=sin(□)inside g=x + 2y

Whythe chain rule in words: "derivative of the outside (leave the inside alone), times the derivative of the inside".

3

Differentiate the inside, x + 2y, with respect to x.

∂∂x[x] =1 ∂∂x[2y] =0total=1 + 0 = 1

Whyx: the derivative of x with respect to x is 1; 2y: there is no x anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as x is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0.

4

Multiply: (derivative of the outside, inside untouched) × (derivative of the inside).

∂∂x[sin(x + 2y)] =cos(x + 2y)·1=cos(x + 2y)
5

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

zy= ∂∂y[sin(x + 2y)]
6

This is a function inside a function: sin of something. The outside is sin(□) and the inside is x + 2y. That means the chain rule.

outside=sin(□)inside g=x + 2y

Whythe chain rule in words: "derivative of the outside (leave the inside alone), times the derivative of the inside".

7

Differentiate the inside, x + 2y, with respect to y.

∂∂y[x] =0 ∂∂y[2y] =2·1total=0 + 2 = 2

Whyx: there is no y anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as y is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0; 2y: 2 has no y, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of y with respect to y is 1.

8

Multiply: (derivative of the outside, inside untouched) × (derivative of the inside).

∂∂y[sin(x + 2y)] =cos(x + 2y)·2=2 cos(x + 2y)
zx = cos(x + 2y)  ·  zy = 2 cos(x + 2y)
Q33z = tan(2x − y)
Question

Find both first partial derivatives zx and zy of z = tan(2x − y).

Think firstBefore any algebra, name the shape. A trig function of something: use the derivative of the trig function, copy the inside unchanged, then multiply by the derivative of the inside. Then do the x-partial with y frozen, and the y-partial with x frozen.
1

We differentiate with respect to x. That means y is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while x is the only thing allowed to move.

zx= ∂∂x[tan(2x − y)]

Whythe partial derivative zx asks: how fast does z change when only x changes?

2

This is a function inside a function: tan of something. The outside is tan(□) and the inside is 2x − y. That means the chain rule.

outside=tan(□)inside g=2x − y

Whythe chain rule in words: "derivative of the outside (leave the inside alone), times the derivative of the inside".

3

Differentiate the inside, 2x − y, with respect to x.

∂∂x[−y] =0 ∂∂x[2x] =2·1total=0 + 2 = 2

Why−y: there is no x anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as x is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0; 2x: 2 has no x, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of x with respect to x is 1.

4

Multiply: (derivative of the outside, inside untouched) × (derivative of the inside).

∂∂x[tan(2x − y)] =tan2(2x − y) + 1·2=2 tan2(2x − y) + 2
5

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

zy= ∂∂y[tan(2x − y)]
6

This is a function inside a function: tan of something. The outside is tan(□) and the inside is 2x − y. That means the chain rule.

outside=tan(□)inside g=2x − y

Whythe chain rule in words: "derivative of the outside (leave the inside alone), times the derivative of the inside".

7

Differentiate the inside, 2x − y, with respect to y.

∂∂y[−y] =(−1)·1 ∂∂y[2x] =0total=−1 + 0 = −1

Why−y: −1 has no y, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of y with respect to y is 1; 2x: there is no y anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as y is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0.

8

Multiply: (derivative of the outside, inside untouched) × (derivative of the inside).

∂∂y[tan(2x − y)] =tan2(2x − y) + 1·(−1)=−tan2(2x − y) − 1
9

Tidy up: the same two answers written in the neatest form (the usual textbook form).

zx=2 tan2(2x − y) + 2=2 sec2(2x − y)zy=−tan2(2x − y) − 1=−sec2(2x − y)

Whyfactoring or combining fractions makes the answer shorter and easier to check, and it matches how the answer key usually looks.

zx = 2 sec2(2x − y)  ·  zy = −sec2(2x − y)
Q34z = sin(5x) cos(5y)
Question

Find both first partial derivatives zx and zy of z = sin(5x) cos(5y).

Think firstBefore any algebra, name the shape. Everything except one piece is frozen, so you are really differentiating a constant × one piece. The constant just rides along. Then do the x-partial with y frozen, and the y-partial with x frozen.
1

We differentiate with respect to x. That means y is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while x is the only thing allowed to move.

zx= ∂∂x[sin(5x) cos(5y)]

Whythe partial derivative zx asks: how fast does z change when only x changes?

2

cos(5y) has no x in it, so it rides along as a multiplier, and only sin(5x) is differentiated.

∂∂x[sin(5x) cos(5y)] =cos(5y)·[cos(5x)·5]=5 cos(5x) cos(5y)

Whycos(5y) has no x, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of sin is cos(q) (inside copied unchanged), and the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of the inside

3

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

zy= ∂∂y[sin(5x) cos(5y)]
4

sin(5x) has no y in it, so it rides along as a multiplier, and only cos(5y) is differentiated.

∂∂y[sin(5x) cos(5y)] =sin(5x)·[−sin(5y)·5]=−5 sin(5x) sin(5y)

Whysin(5x) has no y, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of cos is −sin(q) (inside copied unchanged), and the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of the inside

zx = 5 cos(5x) cos(5y)  ·  zy = −5 sin(5x) sin(5y)
Q35z = ey sin(8xy)
Question

Find both first partial derivatives zx and zy of z = ey sin(8xy).

Think firstBefore any algebra, name the shape. Everything except one piece is frozen, so you are really differentiating a constant × one piece. The constant just rides along. Then do the x-partial with y frozen, and the y-partial with x frozen.
1

We differentiate with respect to x. That means y is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while x is the only thing allowed to move.

zx= ∂∂x[ey sin(8xy)]

Whythe partial derivative zx asks: how fast does z change when only x changes?

2

ey has no x in it, so it rides along as a multiplier, and only sin(8xy) is differentiated.

∂∂x[ey sin(8xy)] =ey·[cos(8xy)·8y]=8yey cos(8xy)

Whyey has no x, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of sin is cos(q) (inside copied unchanged), and the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of the inside

3

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

zy= ∂∂y[ey sin(8xy)]
4

ey and sin(8xy) are multiplied together and both contain y. That is a job for the product rule.

u=eyw=sin(8xy)
∂∂y[u·w] = u′·w + u·w′

Whyboth factors are changing, so each one gets a turn: "derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times the derivative of the second".

5

Differentiate each factor on its own, as if the other was not there.

u′=ey·1=eyw′=cos(8xy)·8x=8x cos(8xy)

Whyfor u: e( ) copies itself, and the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of the exponent. For w: the derivative of sin is cos(q) (inside copied unchanged), and the chain rule multiplies by the derivative of the inside.

6

Drop the pieces into the product rule u′w + uw′ and tidy up.

∂∂y[ey sin(8xy)] =ey·sin(8xy) + ey·8x cos(8xy)=(8x cos(8xy) + sin(8xy))ey
zx = 8yey cos(8xy)  ·  zy = (8x cos(8xy) + sin(8xy))ey
Q36z = cos(x2 + y2)

Find both first partial derivatives zx and zy of z = cos(x2 + y2).

Think firstBefore any algebra, name the shape. A trig function of something: use the derivative of the trig function, copy the inside unchanged, then multiply by the derivative of the inside. Then do the x-partial with y frozen, and the y-partial with x frozen.
1

We differentiate with respect to x. That means y is frozen: treat it like ordinary numbers (a 5 or a 7) while x is the only thing allowed to move.

zx= ∂∂x[cos(x2 + y2)]

Whythe partial derivative zx asks: how fast does z change when only x changes?

2

This is a function inside a function: cos of something. The outside is cos(□) and the inside is x2 + y2. That means the chain rule.

outside=cos(□)inside g=x2 + y2

Whythe chain rule in words: "derivative of the outside (leave the inside alone), times the derivative of the inside".

3

Differentiate the inside, x2 + y2, with respect to x.

∂∂x[x2] =2·x ∂∂x[y2] =0total=2x + 0 = 2x

Whyx2: power rule: bring the exponent down in front, then lower the exponent by 1; y2: there is no x anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as x is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0.

5

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

zy= ∂∂y[cos(x2 + y2)]
6

This is a function inside a function: cos of something. The outside is cos(□) and the inside is x2 + y2. That means the chain rule.

outside=cos(□)inside g=x2 + y2

Whythe chain rule in words: "derivative of the outside (leave the inside alone), times the derivative of the inside".

Differentiate the inside, x2 + y2, with respect to y.

∂∂y[x2] =0 ∂∂y[y2] =2·ytotal=0 + 2y = 2y

Whyx2: there is no y anywhere in it, so it is just a number as far as y is concerned; the derivative of a number is 0; y2: power rule: bring the exponent down in front, then lower the exponent by 1.

8

Multiply: (derivative of the outside, inside untouched) × (derivative of the inside).

∂∂y[cos(x2 + y2)] =−sin(x2 + y2)·2y=−2y sin(x2 + y2)
zx = −2x sin(x2 + y2)  ·  zy = −2y sin(x2 + y2)

outside=sinh(□)inside g=2x + 3y

∂∂x[2x] =2·1 ∂∂x[3y] =0total=2 + 0 = 2

Multiply: (derivative of the outside, inside untouched) × (derivative of the inside).

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

zy= ∂∂y[sinh(2x + 3y)]
6

This is a function inside a function: sinh of something. The outside is sinh(□) and the inside is 2x + 3y. That means the chain rule.

outside=sinh(□)inside g=2x + 3y

Multiply: (derivative of the outside, inside untouched) × (derivative of the inside).

∂∂y[sinh(2x + 3y)] =cosh(2x + 3y)·3=3 cosh(2x + 3y)

1

zx= ∂∂x[cosh(xy2)]

Whythe partial derivative zx asks: how fast does z change when only x changes?

2

This is a function inside a function: cosh of something. The outside is cosh(□) and the inside is xy2. That means the chain rule.

outside=cosh(□)inside g=xy2

Whythe chain rule in words: "derivative of the outside (leave the inside alone), times the derivative of the inside".

3

Differentiate the inside, xy2, with respect to x.

∂∂x[xy2] =y2·1=y2

Whyxy2: y2 has no x, so it just rides along as a multiplier; then the derivative of x with respect to x is 1.

4

Multiply: (derivative of the outside, inside untouched) × (derivative of the inside).

∂∂x[cosh(xy2)] =sinh(xy2)·y2=y2 sinh(xy2)
5

Now with respect to y: this time x is frozen.

zy= ∂∂y[cosh(xy2)]

This is a function inside a function: cosh of something. The outside is cosh(□) and the inside is xy2. That means the chain rule.

outside=cosh(□)inside g=xy2

Q39–Q40 · integral-defined functions
Q39f = ∫xy(t2 − 1)dt
Question

Find fx and fy for f(x, y) = ∫xy(t2 − 1) dt.

Think firstYou should not need to integrate at all: look at which limit holds your letter.
1

Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. For ∫ab g(t) dt: differentiating by the top limit gives g(top), and differentiating by the bottom limit gives −g(bottom).

Whythe integral is the area from a to b. Growing the top adds a sliver of height g(b). Moving the bottom right removes a sliver, hence the minus sign.

Watch outSay it: 'top is +, bottom is −'.

2

Differentiate by y (the top limit): replace t by y in the integrand.

fy=y2 − 1

Whythe letter y sits on top, so it just takes the place of t.

3

Differentiate by x (the bottom limit): same replacement, but with a minus sign.

fx=−(x2 − 1)=1 − x2

Whyx is on the bottom, so the FTC hands us a minus sign.

4

Check by actually integrating first (optional but reassuring).

f=( y33 − y) − (x33 − x)fy=y2 − 1fx=−x2 + 1

Whydoing it the long way gives the same two answers, so the shortcut is trustworthy.

fx = 1 − x2  ·  fy = y2 − 1
Q40f = ∫xy(2t + 1)dt + ∫yx(2t − 1)dt
Question

Find fx and fy for f(x, y) = ∫xy(2t + 1) dt + ∫yx(2t − 1) dt.

Think firstTwo integrals, so work out the sign for each limit separately and then add.
1

There are two integrals. We differentiate each one by the FTC rule (top is +, bottom is −) and then add.

Whythe derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives.

Watch outWrite the integrand first, then decide the sign from the position of the letter.

2

Differentiate by x. In the first integral x is the bottom limit; in the second integral x is the top limit.

fx=−(2x + 1) + (2x − 1)=−2x − 1 + 2x − 1=−2

Whybottom gives minus, top gives plus. The 2x terms cancel.

3

Differentiate by y. In the first integral y is the top limit; in the second y is the bottom limit.

fy=(2y + 1) − (2y − 1)=2y + 1 − 2y + 1=2

Whytop gives plus, bottom gives minus. This time the 2y terms cancel.

4

Check by integrating first.

f=(y2 + y − x2 − x) + (x2 − x − y2 + y)=2y − 2xfx, fy=−2, 2

Whythe whole thing collapses to the plane 2y − 2x, whose slopes are indeed −2 and 2.

fx = −2  ·  fy = 2
Q41–Q44 · limit definition
Q41f = 3x + 2y
Question

Use the limit definition to find fx and fy for f(x, y) = 3x + 2y.

Think firstExpand f(x + Δx, y), subtract f(x, y), and watch almost everything cancel.
1

Write the limit definition of the partial derivative, one letter at a time.

fx=limΔx→0 f(x + Δx, y) − f(x, y)Δx fy=limΔy→0 f(x, y + Δy) − f(x, y)Δy

Whythis is the one-variable definition of the derivative, nudging only one letter. The other letter stays exactly where it is.

Watch outNever plug in Δ = 0 straight away. You always get 0/0. Simplify first.

2

x-direction: build the top of the fraction, f(x + Δx, y) − f(x, y).

top=(3(x + Δx) + 2y) − (3x + 2y)=3x + 3Δx + 2y − 3x − 2y=3Δx÷ Δx= 3ΔxΔx = 3

Whyeverything cancels except the piece that carries Δx.

3

y-direction: the same, but nudge y.

top=(3x + 2(y + Δy)) − (3x + 2y)=2Δy÷ Δy= 2ΔyΔy = 2

Whysame idea; only 2y changes when y moves.

4

Finish: cancel the small number from top and bottom, then let it shrink to 0.

fx=3fy=2

Whyonce the common factor is cancelled there is nothing left to divide by 0, so we may safely let Δ → 0.

fx = 3  ·  fy = 2
Q42f = x2 − 2xy + y2
Question

Use the limit definition to find fx and fy for f(x, y) = x2 − 2xy + y2.

Think firstExpand squares carefully; every surviving term must contain the small number.
1

Write the limit definition of the partial derivative, one letter at a time.

fx=limΔx→0 f(x + Δx, y) − f(x, y)Δx fy=limΔy→0 f(x, y + Δy) − f(x, y)Δy

Whythis is the one-variable definition of the derivative, nudging only one letter. The other letter stays exactly where it is.

Watch outNever plug in Δ = 0 straight away. You always get 0/0. Simplify first.

2

x-direction: build the top of the fraction, f(x + Δx, y) − f(x, y).

f(x + Δx, y)=(x + Δx)2 − 2(x + Δx)y + y2=x2 + 2xΔx + (Δx)2 − 2xy − 2yΔx + y2top=2xΔx + (Δx)2 − 2yΔx÷ Δx=2x + Δx − 2y

Whyafter subtracting f(x, y) every term that has no Δx cancels. What is left all contains Δx, so Δx factors out.

3

y-direction: the same, but nudge y.

f(x, y + Δy)=x2 − 2x(y + Δy) + (y + Δy)2=x2 − 2xy − 2xΔy + y2 + 2yΔy + (Δy)2top=−2xΔy + 2yΔy + (Δy)2÷ Δy=−2x + 2y + Δy

Whysame method in y. Expand (y + Δy)² carefully: it is y² + 2yΔy + (Δy)².

4

Finish: cancel the small number from top and bottom, then let it shrink to 0.

fx=2x − 2yfy=−2x + 2y

Whyonce the common factor is cancelled there is nothing left to divide by 0, so we may safely let Δ → 0.

fx = 2x − 2y  ·  fy = −2x + 2y
Q43f = √x + y
Question

Use the limit definition to find fx and fy for f(x, y) = √x + y.

Think firstA root minus a root over a small number: multiply by the conjugate.
1

Write the limit definition for fx.

fx=limΔx→0 √x + Δx + y − √x + yΔx

Whysame definition as always: nudge x by Δx and compare.

2

If we put Δx = 0 we get 0/0. A square root difference is a classic case: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate.

conjugate=√x + Δx + y + √x + y

Whythe conjugate turns (A − B)(A + B) into A² − B², which kills the square roots on top.

Watch outWhenever the top is 'root minus root' and you are stuck at 0/0, think conjugate.

3

Multiply out the top.

=lim (x + Δx + y) − (x + y)Δx(√x + Δx + y + √x + y) =lim ΔxΔx(√x + Δx + y + √x + y)

Why(A − B)(A + B) = A² − B², so the square roots vanish and the top simplifies to exactly Δx.

4

Cancel Δx, then let Δx → 0.

=lim 1√x + Δx + y + √x + y= 1√x + y + √x + y = 12√x + y

Whyafter cancelling there is no 0/0 left, so we just substitute Δx = 0.

5

The y-direction: y enters only through x + y, exactly like x does, so the same steps with Δy give the same answer.

fy= 12√x + y

Whythe function depends on x and y only through their sum, so both partials are equal.

fx = fy = 12√x + y
Q44f = 1x + y
Question

Use the limit definition to find fx and fy for f(x, y) = 1x + y.

Think firstA fraction minus a fraction: put them over a common denominator first.
1

Write the limit definition.

fx=limΔx→0 1x + Δx + y − 1x + y Δx

Whysame pattern as the others: nudge x and compare.

2

Combine the two fractions on top over a common denominator.

top= (x + y) − (x + Δx + y)(x + Δx + y)(x + y) = −Δx(x + Δx + y)(x + y)

Whyyou cannot cancel anything while there are fractions inside fractions. A common denominator turns the top into one clean fraction, and the Δx appears on top.

3

Divide by Δx: the Δx cancels.

=lim −1(x + Δx + y)(x + y)

Whydividing a fraction by Δx just puts another Δx under it, which cancels the Δx on top.

4

Let Δx → 0.

fx= −1(x + y)(x + y) =−1(x + y)2

Whyno 0/0 remains, so we substitute Δx = 0.

5

The y-direction: the same steps with Δy (y enters only through x + y).

fy=− 1(x + y)2

Whythe function depends on x + y only, so both slopes agree.

fx = fy = −1(x + y)2
6
13.3 · Q45–56

Evaluating partials and slopes of a surface

Toolkit rules for this sectionEvaluateChainTrigExact valuesQuotientFraction tricks

The slope of a surface at the point (x0, y0, z0) is read from the partials: fx(x0, y0) is the slope in the x-direction, fy(x0, y0) in the y-direction. Positive: surface rising as you move in that direction; negative: falling; zero: flat (possible peak, pit or saddle).

Step-by-step method

  1. Find the general partials fx, fy first (all letters still in the formula).
  2. Substitute the point last. Use only the x and y coordinates; for Q53–56 the z-value is just a check that the point lies on the surface.
  3. Simplify using exact values (sin(π/6) = ½, eln 3 = 3).
  4. State the two numbers with a sentence (“slope in the x-direction is …”) when the exercise asks for slopes.
Exercises Task Tip
Q45–48, 51, 52 Find fx, fy and evaluate at a point Differentiate fully, then substitute
Q53–56 Slopes of a surface at a point (x, y, z) Same as above; ignore z in the formulas

Substituting the point first. Plugging (x, y) into f before differentiating turns f into a constant, and every derivative becomes 0. Differentiate with the letters still in, then substitute.

Worked examples

EasySlopes of z = xyQ53
Question

Find the slopes of z = xy in the x- and y-directions at (1, 2, 2).

  1. zx = y and zy = x.

13.3 · Q57–68

Partial derivatives of functions of three variables

Toolkit rules for this sectionPartial defRadical sumChainLog lawsQuotientEvaluate

Three variables change nothing in the method: for fx treat y and z as constants; for fy freeze x and z; for fz freeze x and y. The only extra work is bookkeeping, so write the three answers on three separate lines.

Step-by-step method

  1. Rewrite roots and reciprocals as powers; split logs.
  2. Differentiate three times, announcing the frozen letters each time.
  3. Check by symmetry: if the formula treats x, y, z alike (like √x2 + y2 + z2), the three answers must look alike.
  4. For evaluation questions (Q63–68) plug the point in after differentiating, and simplify exact values.
Exercises Task
Q57–62 All three first partials
Q63–68 All three first partials, evaluated at a point

Radical sum trick: w = √x2 + y2 + z2 gives wx = xw, wy = yw, wz = zw. And ln√x2 + y2 + z2 = ½ln(x2 + y2 + z2) gives xx2 + y2 + z2 , … the ½ cancels the 2 from the chain rule.

13.3 · Q69–76

Critical points: solving fx = 0 and fy = 0 together

Toolkit rules for this sectionCritical ptsDomain

Where both slopes are zero, fx = 0 and fy = 0, the tangent plane is horizontal. Those critical points are the only candidates for peaks, pits and saddle points. The exercise is purely algebra: set up the two equations and solve them simultaneously.

Step-by-step method

  1. Compute fx and fy.
  2. Write the system fx = 0, fy = 0.
  3. Solve it: linear system → substitution or elimination. Non-linear → solve one equation for one variable, substitute into the other, factor.
  4. If the function has an exponential factor like ex² + xy + y², it is never 0, so only the other factor matters.
  5. Check every candidate in both equations and reject any that break the domain (for example x = 0 in 1/x).
Exercises System type
Q69–72 Linear (quadratic function): elimination
Q73 Reciprocals: substitute y = 1/x2
Q74 Cubic: substitute and factor
Q75, Q76 Exponential or log of a quadratic: only the inner derivative can vanish

Nonlinear systems often have more than one solution. After substituting you get something like x(x3 − 1) = 0: do not divide by x and lose x = 0. Then decide separately whether each root is allowed by the original function.

Only the point (0, 0).

13.3 · Q77–85, 91–94

Second and higher-order partial derivatives

Toolkit rules for this sectionHigher-orderProductChainRadical sum

Second partials are just partials of partials. There are four in two variables: fxx, fyy, fxy, fyx. Read the subscripts left to right: fxy = (fx)y means “differentiate in x first, then y”. The fraction form runs right to left: ∂²f∂y∂x also means x first, then y. Theorem 13.3: if fxy and fyx are continuous, they are equal, so every exercise has a free built-in check.

Step-by-step method

  1. Find fx and fy and simplify them before going on.
  2. Differentiate fx with respect to x (fxx) and y (fxy); differentiate fy with respect to y (fyy) and x (fyx).
  3. Compare fxy and fyx. If they differ, one of the two has an algebra slip.
  4. Third order (Q91–94): differentiate three times in the order of the subscripts. fxyy = x, then y, then y.
Exercises Task
Q77–85 All four second partials; observe the mixed ones agree
Q91–94 Show fxyy = fyxy = fyyx

Differentiating a product like x4 twice? Do not expand a messy fx until the last step; and when a letter is missing from fx (like y in 3y2), the mixed partial is just the derivative of what is there.

Mixing up the order of fxy and ∂²f∂x∂y . They look the same but mean opposite orders. Fortunately Theorem 13.3 makes the numerical answer identical for nice functions, so only your notation can go wrong.

13.3 · Q123–124

Applications: partial derivatives as rates of change

Toolkit rules for this sectionUnitsEvaluate

In applied problems a partial derivative is a rate of change. Its units are (units of the output) per (unit of the input you vary), and its sign says whether the output rises or falls as that input increases, with the other inputs held fixed. Say it in a sentence with units.

Step-by-step method

  1. Identify the quantity (output) and the variable you move (input); everything else is frozen.
  2. Differentiate with respect to that variable only.
  3. Substitute the given point. Keep the units: output unit ÷ input unit.
  4. Interpret in words: “at this point, increasing x by one unit changes T by about …”.
Exercise Task
Q123 Temperature on a steel plate: rates in the x and y directions
Q124 Apparent temperature: rates in t and h, then compare their effects

Worked examples

  2. At (2, 3): ∂T∂x = −1.2(2) = −2.4 and ∂T∂y = −3(3) = −9 .
  3. Units: degrees (temperature units) per metre.
∂T∂x = −2.4 per metre, ∂T∂y = −9 per metre. Moving along either axis away from the origin the plate cools, much faster in the y-direction.

  1. ∂A∂t = 0.885 + 1.20h (the product 1.20th gives 1.20h when t moves).
  2. ∂A∂h = −22.4 + 1.20t .
  3. Substitute: 0.885 + 1.20(0.80) = 0.885 + 0.96 = 1.845 and −22.4 + 1.20(30) = −22.4 + 36 = 13.6.
∂A∂t = 1.845 (°C of apparent temperature per °C of air temperature)  ·  ∂A∂h = 13.6 (°C per unit of humidity)
HardWhich variable matters more?Q124 (b)
Question

Decide whether air temperature or humidity has the greater effect on A, and defend it.

  1. Textbook comparison: 13.6 > 1.845, so A is more sensitive to h (per unit of h).
  2. Sanity check on units: h is a decimal, so one “unit” of h is 100% humidity, an unrealistic change. A 1% change is Δh = 0.01 and gives ΔA ≈ 13.6 × 0.01 = 0.136°C, while a 1° change in air temperature gives ΔA ≈ 1.845°C.
  3. So per the partial derivatives alone humidity wins; per realistic everyday changes air temperature clearly has the bigger effect.
State the partial-derivative comparison (humidity: 13.6 > 1.845) and mention the units caveat; that earns full credit and shows understanding.

Comparing two partials without checking their units or scales. A bigger number does not automatically mean a bigger practical effect if the inputs are measured in different-sized units.

13.4 · Q3–8

The total differential

Toolkit rules for this sectionTotal differentialQuotientChain

For z = f(x, y) the increments Δx, Δy are real changes in the inputs and Δz = f(x + Δx, y + Δy) − f(x, y) is the exact change in output. The differentials are dx = Δx, dy = Δy and the total differential

dz = ∂z∂x dx + ∂z∂y dy = fx(x, y) dx + fy(x, y) dy

With three variables just add a term: dw = wx dx + wy dy + wz dz. For small increments Δz ≈ dz (a linear approximation: the surface is replaced by its tangent plane).

Step-by-step method

  1. Compute each first partial of the function (with respect to every variable).
  2. Multiply each partial by its differential (dx, dy, dz) and add.
  3. Keep the differentials as symbols; do not plug in numbers unless the question gives a point.
  4. Sanity check: the number of terms equals the number of variables (some may be zero but look for them).
Exercises Task
Q3–6 Total differential of z = f(x, y)
Q7, Q8 Total differential of w = f(x, y, z)

Write the answer as (…) dx + (…) dy + (…) dz and double-check every bracket against the partial you computed. In Q8 the variable y appears in two places (top and bottom), so wy needs the quotient rule.

Confusing dz with Δz. Δz is the true change; dz is the tangent-plane estimate. They are close only when Δx and Δy are small.

  2. Multiply by the differentials and add.
